patient.name: Gloria Adeyemi
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then acute medical unit
patient.complaint: Four days of diarrhoea and vomiting, now dizzy and passing very little urine
background: Knee osteoarthritis: buying ibuprofen over the counter
Baseline creatinine 92 µmol/L three months ago
Lives alone in Peckham; daughter visits daily

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely cause' with a rising creatinine: decide pre-renal, intrinsic (usually ATN) or post-renal from the history, examination and urine. Classic distractors are the other two categories.

points: Gloria, 77, four days of **diarrhoea and vomiting**.
Kept taking ramipril, furosemide, metformin **and ibuprofen**.
Dizzy on standing; passed a little dark urine today.

steps.lead: Gloria's creatinine has risen sharply over days and her urine output has dropped: a **sudden decline** in renal function.
Gloria has stacked precipitants: **dehydration**, an **ACE inhibitor**, a diuretic and an **NSAID**.

steps.title: Bloods on arrival
steps.text: Urea has risen far more than creatinine, the pattern of **pre-renal** AKI. Calcium is normal, which fits an acute rather than chronic problem.

steps.lead: Gloria is **oliguric** and her normal calcium supports an **acute** injury: hypocalcaemia would hint at underlying CKD.

steps.q: Which category of AKI fits Gloria best?
steps.r: Fluid loss, hypotension, tachycardia, dry mucosa and a urea rise out of proportion to creatinine = **pre-renal**.

steps.lead: Gloria fits **pre-renal** AKI; untreated hypoperfusion can progress to **ATN**, and an elderly man with a big bladder would point to post-renal.

visual.title: The post-renal clue to feel for
visual.caption: Gloria's suprapubic area is soft and non-tender. A **palpable, tender bladder** would point to post-renal AKI (most often BPH in men).

steps.lead: Gloria has no CK rise or crush history, but **rhabdomyolysis** after a long lie is a classic AKI cause; overloading her with fluid would give **crackles and oedema**.

steps.text: A creatinine rise **soon after starting an ACE inhibitor** is not just 'pre-renal': think **renal artery stenosis**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?': U&Es to show the rise, then renal tract ultrasound within 24 hours for unexplained AKI. Staging questions give a baseline creatinine and ask the stage.

steps.lead: Gloria's **U&Es** show the rising creatinine; a **blood gas** shows her acidosis and potassium within minutes.
Gloria's creatinine has risen from 92 to 318 in days: well past the **26 µmol/L in 48 hours** and **50% in 7 days** thresholds.

steps.q: Baseline 92, now 318 µmol/L. What AKI stage is Gloria?
steps.r: 318 ÷ 92 = **3.5 times baseline**, which is **Stage 3** (3 times baseline or more).

visual.title: Creatinine as a multiple of baseline
visual.label: Gloria 3.5×
visual.caption: Use whichever criterion (creatinine or urine output) gives the **highest** stage.

steps.lead: Gloria is **Stage 3** on creatinine; her urine output would only need to fall below 0.3 mL/kg/hr for 24 h to reach the same stage.
On examination Gloria is **dry, hypotensive and tachycardic**: no crackles, oedema or palpable bladder. Her ramipril has gone unmonitored.

points: Urine dip: no blood, protein trace, no leucocytes.

steps.lead: Gloria's cause seems clear, but if she fails to improve she gets a **USS KUB within 24 hours**; blood or protein on dip would prompt a **renal screen**.

steps.title: Investigating AKI
nodes: Blood gas, FBC, CRP; ECG if K high
USS KUB within 24 h if unexplained
Blood/protein on dip → renal screen (ANCA, anti-GBM, C3/C4, ANA)

steps.text: AKI is defined by the **rise from baseline**, not by one creatinine value. Always find the previous result before staging.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': assess fluid status, give IV 0.9% saline if dry, stop nephrotoxic drugs (DAMN), protect the heart if potassium is high, and escalate to dialysis using AEIOU.

visual.title: Gloria's ECG (K+ 6.8 mmol/L)
visual.caption: Tall, **tented T waves** across the precordial leads: hyperkalaemia with ECG changes.

steps.q: Gloria's K+ is 6.8 with tented T waves. What is given first?
steps.r: **IV calcium gluconate** stabilises the cardiac membrane within minutes. Insulin-dextrose then shifts potassium into cells.

steps.lead: Gloria's **ramipril, furosemide, metformin and ibuprofen** all stop (DAMN), and she is dry, so she gets **IV 0.9% saline**.

steps.text: **DAMN** drugs to stop: Diuretics (and digoxin), ACE inhibitor/ARB, Metformin (and methotrexate), NSAIDs. Keep cardioprotective **aspirin**; warfarin is usually safe.

steps.lead: Gloria's cause is fluid loss, so **fluids** treat it. Her potassium is treated, then **U&Es and urine output** are watched closely.

points: 500 mL 0.9% saline bolus, then reassessed: BP 108/64.
Next morning she is passing 40 mL/hour.

steps.text: A brisk fall in creatinine after fluids confirms **pre-renal** AKI. ATN would respond poorly.

steps.title: Treat the cause
head: Type
Treatment
rows: IV fluids (0.9% saline); stop DAMN drugs

steps.lead: Had Gloria stayed anuric with **K+ above 7**, pH below 7.20 or pulmonary oedema, she would need **dialysis** (AEIOU).
Gloria's care uses the **AKI staging criteria** to grade her and the **AEIOU** list to decide that she does not need dialysis.

science.exam: Science questions ask why pre-renal urine is concentrated, why ATN gives high urinary sodium and casts, why ACE inhibitors drop GFR, and why AKI causes hyperkalaemia and acidosis.

steps.lead: Gloria's kidneys were underperfused, so **RAAS** made them hold on to every bit of sodium and water: concentrated urine, low urinary sodium.

steps.title: Pre-renal physiology
nodes: Fluid loss → low renal blood flow
Slow tubular flow → more urea reabsorbed
steps.caption: This is why urea rises more than creatinine.

steps.lead: If Gloria's hypotension had lasted, her tubular cells would have died: they stop reabsorbing sodium and slough off as **muddy brown casts**.
Obstruction raises pressure in the tubules and cancels the **filtration gradient**; a catheter relieves it.
Gloria's ramipril **relaxed her efferent arterioles** just when angiotensin II was holding up her glomerular pressure, so her GFR fell further.

steps.q: Why did ramipril worsen Gloria's GFR while she was dehydrated?
o: Efferent arteriole dilatation lowers glomerular pressure
steps.r: ACE inhibitors reduce **efferent arteriolar tone**, so glomerular filtration pressure falls in hypoperfusion.

steps.lead: Gloria's kidneys could not excrete **potassium or acid**, causing her K+ of 6.8, tented T waves and bicarbonate of 16.

steps.text: Calcium gluconate **does not lower potassium**. It stabilises the myocardium; insulin-dextrose and dialysis lower the level.

mcq.q: What is the most common category of AKI?
What is the most common cause of post-renal AKI?
Which urine finding suggests acute tubular necrosis?
mcq.r: **Muddy brown casts** from sloughed tubular cells; FeNa >1%, osmolality <350.

mcq.q: Which blood result suggests the kidney disease is chronic rather than acute?
Which creatinine rise in 48 hours defines AKI?
mcq.r: **>26 µmol/L in 48 h**, or >50% in 7 days, or UO <0.5 mL/kg/hr for >6 h.

mcq.q: What is the first-line imaging for unexplained AKI, and how soon?
mcq.r: **Renal tract ultrasound within 24 hours** to exclude obstruction.

mcq.q: Creatinine is 2.5 times baseline. Which AKI stage is this?
Which drug is usually continued in AKI?
mcq.r: DAMN drugs stop; **cardioprotective aspirin** continues (and warfarin is usually safe).

mcq.q: Which potassium level is an indication for dialysis if persistent?
Why does urea rise more than creatinine in pre-renal AKI?
o: Slow tubular flow increases urea reabsorption
Urea production by the liver rises

prompts.q: What are the common precipitants of AKI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem usually hides two or three; list fluid, infection, drugs and background.

points.why: Most common route to pre-renal AKI.

points.p: Nephrotoxic drugs: ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, gentamicin

prompts.q: How do you recognise pre-renal AKI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: dry patient, low BP, urea out of proportion, concentrated urine.

points.p: Reduced perfusion: dehydration, bleeding, heart failure, sepsis, shock
Dry mucous membranes, hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria

points.why: The kidney is still working and concentrating.
Slow tubular flow increases urea reabsorption.

prompts.q: Which features tell you it is intrinsic AKI (ATN) rather than pre-renal?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the urine and the fluid challenge decide it.

points.why: Red cell casts suggest glomerulonephritis instead.

prompts.q: How does post-renal AKI present and what causes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: older man, retention, palpable bladder.

points.p: Obstruction: BPH most common, also stones and tumours
points.why: Bilateral or single-kidney obstruction is needed.

points.p: Acute urinary retention, inability to pass urine

points.why: Elderly patients may present only with confusion.

prompts.q: Which special causes and complications of AKI should you recognise?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: long lie with dark urine; creatinine jump after ACE inhibitor; crackles after fluids.

points.p: Rhabdomyolysis: very high CK, treat with rapid IV fluids
points.why: Classic after a long lie or crush injury.

points.p: Creatinine rise after starting ACE inhibitor: renal artery stenosis
points.why: Bilateral RAS is the classic exam cause.
Refractory pulmonary oedema is a dialysis indication.
Check an ECG if K+ is high.

prompts.q: What defines AKI and how is it staged?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: compare with baseline; use the highest stage from either criterion.

points.p: Or urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/hr for > 6 hours
Stage 3: 3 times baseline or ≥ 354 µmol/L, UO < 0.3 for 24 h or anuria 12 h

prompts.q: Which investigations do you do in AKI, and when?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'first-line' = U&Es; 'unexplained' = USS KUB within 24 h.

points.why: Shows the rising creatinine and potassium.
Gas gives potassium and pH fast.
Blood and protein suggest a glomerular cause.

points.p: USS KUB within 24 h if unexplained
Renal screen if glomerular cause suspected

prompts.q: What is the first-line management of AKI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fluid status first, then drugs, then cause.

points.why: Dry or overloaded decides fluids or diuretics.

points.p: Stop DAMN drugs: diuretics, ACE inhibitor/ARB, metformin, NSAIDs

points.why: Hourly urine output via catheter in severe AKI.

prompts.q: When is dialysis needed in AKI (AEIOU)?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: refractory to medical treatment, with numbers.

points.why: Pericarditis pain is relieved by sitting forward.

prompts.q: Why does pre-renal AKI give concentrated urine, and ATN give high urinary sodium?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: working tubules hold sodium; dead tubules lose it.

points.p: Pre-renal: RAAS activation, avid sodium and water retention
ATN: injured tubular cells cannot reabsorb sodium
Sloughed tubular cells form muddy brown casts

prompts.q: Why do ACE inhibitors worsen AKI, and why does AKI cause hyperkalaemia and acidosis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: efferent arteriole; kidney excretes potassium and acid.

points.p: ACE inhibitors reduce efferent arteriolar tone, lowering GFR in hypoperfusion
Kidney is the main route of potassium excretion
points.why: Hyperkalaemia depolarises cardiac myocytes: tented T waves, arrhythmia.

points.p: IV calcium gluconate stabilises the myocardium
Acidosis: kidneys cannot excrete acid or regenerate bicarbonate

glossary.AKI: Acute kidney injury: a sudden fall in kidney function shown by rising creatinine or reduced urine output.
glossary.Creatinine: A muscle breakdown product cleared by the kidneys; a rising level means falling kidney function.
glossary.Urea: A waste product of protein breakdown cleared by the kidneys; rises disproportionately in pre-renal AKI.
glossary.Baseline creatinine: The patient's usual creatinine before the illness, used to define and stage AKI.
glossary.Oliguria: Low urine output, defined in AKI as less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour.
glossary.Oliguric: Passing less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour of urine.
glossary.Pre-renal: AKI caused by reduced blood flow to otherwise healthy kidneys.
glossary.Intrinsic: AKI caused by damage within the kidney itself, such as ATN or glomerulonephritis.
glossary.Post-renal: AKI caused by obstruction to urine flow after the kidneys, such as BPH or stones.
glossary.ATN: Acute tubular necrosis: death of tubular cells from ischaemia or toxins; the commonest intrinsic AKI.
glossary.Acute tubular necrosis: Death of kidney tubular cells from prolonged low blood pressure, sepsis or nephrotoxins.
glossary.Muddy brown casts: Granular casts of dead tubular cells seen on urine microscopy in ATN.
glossary.FeNa: Fractional excretion of sodium: the share of filtered sodium passed in urine; above 1% suggests ATN.
glossary.Urine osmolality: How concentrated the urine is; above 500 mOsm/kg suggests pre-renal AKI.
glossary.Fluid challenge: A rapid IV fluid bolus, usually 250 to 500 mL, given to see whether perfusion and urine output improve.
glossary.Nephrotoxic: Harmful to the kidneys, as with NSAIDs, gentamicin and contrast agents.
glossary.DAMN: Drugs to stop in AKI: Diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, Metformin, NSAIDs.
glossary.AEIOU: Dialysis indications: Acidosis, Electrolytes (K+), Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia.
glossary.ACE inhibitor: A blood pressure drug such as ramipril that blocks angiotensin II formation and dilates the efferent arteriole.
glossary.ARB: Angiotensin receptor blocker, such as losartan; acts like an ACE inhibitor on the kidney.
glossary.NSAID: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, such as ibuprofen, which constricts the afferent arteriole.
glossary.Gentamicin: An aminoglycoside antibiotic that is toxic to kidney tubules.
glossary.Trimethoprim: An antibiotic that raises creatinine and potassium by blocking tubular secretion.
glossary.Gadolinium: A contrast agent used in MRI that can harm kidneys.
glossary.RAAS: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system: hormones that retain salt and water when kidney perfusion falls.
glossary.Efferent arteriole: The small artery leaving the glomerulus; its tone keeps filtration pressure up.
glossary.Afferent arteriole: The small artery bringing blood into the glomerulus.
glossary.GFR: Glomerular filtration rate: how much blood the kidneys filter per minute.
glossary.Renal artery stenosis: Narrowing of the artery to a kidney; creatinine jumps when an ACE inhibitor is started.
glossary.Rhabdomyolysis: Muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin and CK, which can cause AKI; seen after long lies or crush injury.
glossary.CK: Creatine kinase: a muscle enzyme that is very high in rhabdomyolysis.
glossary.BPH: Benign prostatic hyperplasia: non-cancerous prostate enlargement, the commonest cause of post-renal AKI.
glossary.USS KUB: Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureters and bladder, used to look for obstruction.
glossary.Hydronephrosis: Swelling of the kidney's collecting system from blocked urine flow.
glossary.Renal screen: Blood tests for glomerular causes: ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, dsDNA, C3, C4, immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis.
glossary.ANCA: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, found in small-vessel vasculitis that can cause glomerulonephritis.
glossary.Anti-GBM: Antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane, found in Goodpasture's disease.
glossary.Hyperkalaemia: A high blood potassium level, dangerous because it can cause fatal arrhythmias.
glossary.Tented T waves: Tall, narrow, peaked T waves on ECG, an early sign of hyperkalaemia.
glossary.Calcium gluconate: IV calcium given to stabilise the heart muscle in severe hyperkalaemia; it does not lower potassium.
glossary.Haemofiltration: A form of renal replacement therapy that filters blood continuously, often on ICU.
glossary.Uraemia: Build-up of waste products in the blood, causing nausea, confusion, pericarditis and a grey-brown skin tinge.
glossary.Uraemic pericarditis: Pericardial inflammation from uraemia; chest pain relieved by sitting forward and a dialysis indication.
glossary.Metabolic acidosis: Low blood pH from excess acid or lost bicarbonate, shown by a low bicarbonate.

technique.stem: A 68 year old woman is treated with intravenous gentamicin and amoxicillin for pyelonephritis. On day 6 her urine output falls and her creatinine has risen from 84 µmol/L to 236 µmol/L. She is well hydrated and her BP is 132/78 mmHg. A 500 mL fluid challenge produces no rise in urine output. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown casts.
technique.q: Which is the most likely cause of her acute kidney injury?

steps.x: Cause of AKI: decide the category, then the culprit.

clues: creatinine has risen from 84 µmol/L to 236 µmol/L
steps.x: Nephrotoxin, no response to fluids, and **muddy brown casts** = intrinsic ATN.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gentamicin-induced ATN**.

elim: Interstitial nephritis gives white cell casts, rash and eosinophilia, not muddy brown casts.
Obstruction gives retention and a palpable bladder; casts point to tubules.
She is well hydrated and did not respond to fluid.
RAS presents after an ACE inhibitor, with bland urine.

steps.x: **C. Gentamicin-induced ATN.** Rule: nephrotoxin + muddy brown casts + no fluid response = ATN.

technique.stem: An 82 year old man is found on his kitchen floor after lying there for about 2 days. His urine is dark brown. His temperature is 36.1°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 106/64 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ but microscopy shows no red cells.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause of his acute kidney injury?

steps.x: The test that finds the cause of the AKI.
Long lie, dark urine, dipstick blood without red cells (**myoglobin**): rhabdomyolysis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Plasma CK**: markedly raised in rhabdomyolysis.

elim: Anti-GBM is for haemoptysis with glomerulonephritis.
Biopsy is invasive and not first for an obvious cause.
Amylase is for pancreatitis.
Culture finds infection; no red cells with heavy blood points to myoglobin.

steps.x: **B. Plasma creatine kinase.** Rule: long lie + dark urine + dip blood without red cells = check CK.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man with acute kidney injury is waiting for a central venous catheter to be inserted. He takes ramipril and spironolactone. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 142/80 mmHg. ECG (see item resources).
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Stop ramipril and recheck in 24 hours

steps.x: Immediate management before a procedure.
K+ 7.1 with **tented T waves** before line insertion: the heart is at risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV calcium gluconate** to stabilise the myocardium, then insulin-dextrose.

elim: Furosemide is slow and he may not respond in AKI.
Calcium resonium works over hours to days.
Oral bicarbonate is not the emergency step.
Stopping drugs is right but far too slow alone.

steps.x: **A. IV calcium gluconate.** Rule: high K+ with ECG changes = calcium gluconate first.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man with hypertension and peripheral arterial disease is started on ramipril. Two weeks later his creatinine has risen from 98 µmol/L to 186 µmol/L. Renal artery Doppler shows bilateral renal artery stenosis.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the fall in his glomerular filtration rate?

steps.x: Mechanism of ACE inhibitor-related GFR fall.

clues: creatinine has risen from 98 µmol/L to 186 µmol/L
steps.x: With RAS, glomerular pressure depends on **angiotensin II constricting the efferent arteriole**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ACE inhibitor removes **efferent arteriolar tone**, so filtration pressure drops.

elim: Afferent constriction is how NSAIDs harm GFR.
Tubular toxicity is gentamicin-type ATN.
Interstitial nephritis is an allergic drug reaction (e.g. PPIs, penicillins).
No obstruction is shown.

steps.x: **D. Loss of efferent arteriolar tone.** Rule: ACE inhibitor = efferent; NSAID = afferent.

practice.stem: An 80 year old woman has had diarrhoea for 5 days. She takes lisinopril and bendroflumethiazide. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 94/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fluid loss, hypotension, a disproportionate urea rise, concentrated urine and low urinary sodium are pre-renal AKI.

steps.x: Type of AKI.
Dehydrated, on ACE inhibitor and diuretic; urea high, urine osmolality **>500**, low urine sodium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pre-renal AKI**.

elim: AIN follows a drug reaction with rash, fever and white cells in urine.
ATN gives dilute urine (<350) and high urine sodium.
No retention or palpable bladder.
RPGN gives blood and protein on dip with a systemic illness.

steps.x: **D. Pre-renal AKI.** Rule: dry + urea up more than creatinine + osmolality >500 = pre-renal.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man is on ICU after 3 days of septic shock from a perforated bowel. He needed noradrenaline for 48 hours. His urine output remains 10 mL/hour despite 2 litres of fluid. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown casts. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 118/68 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Prolonged hypotension, no response to fluids, muddy brown casts, FeNa >1% and dilute urine are ATN.

steps.x: Type of AKI after shock.
Prolonged hypoperfusion, no fluid response, casts; FeNa 3.2%, osmolality 290.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute tubular necrosis**.

elim: No retention; he is catheterised on ICU with casts in the urine.
No contrast mentioned; casts and shock explain it.
Hepatorenal needs liver failure and gives low urine sodium.
Pre-renal responds to fluid, with osmolality >500 and FeNa <1%.

steps.x: **A. ATN.** Rule: muddy brown casts + FeNa >1% + no fluid response.

practice.stem: A 79 year old man has not passed urine for 14 hours and has severe lower abdominal pain. For 1 year he has had a poor stream and nocturia. A tender mass is palpable above the pubic symphysis, dull to percussion. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his acute kidney injury?
practice.e: Acute retention with a palpable bladder and long-standing poor stream is post-renal AKI from BPH, the commonest cause.

steps.x: Cause of AKI.
Acute urinary retention and LUTS: **post-renal**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **BPH** causing obstruction.

elim: ATN does not cause a palpable, painful bladder.
RAS follows an ACE inhibitor and does not cause retention.
He is hypertensive, not dry.
UTI gives dysuria and fever; it is not the cause of obstruction here.

steps.x: **B. BPH.** Rule: retention + palpable bladder in an older man = post-renal from BPH.

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman with oliguric acute kidney injury has been given 4 litres of intravenous fluid over 24 hours. She is now breathless lying flat. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 156/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Absent breath sounds at the left apex
Bronchial breathing at the right base
practice.e: Excess fluid in an oliguric patient causes fluid overload: pulmonary oedema with bibasal crackles and peripheral oedema.

steps.x: A finding on examination.
Fluid in, no urine out, orthopnoea, hypoxia: **fluid overload**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bibasal crackles** of pulmonary oedema.

elim: Absent apical breath sounds suggest pneumothorax, not overload.
Bronchial breathing is consolidation, which is unilateral.
She is overloaded, not dry.
Nothing suggests obstruction.

steps.x: **B. Bibasal crackles.** Rule: oliguric + lots of fluid + breathless = overload.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and peripheral vascular disease was started on ramipril 10 days ago. He feels well. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. A renal bruit is heard.
practice.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his acute kidney injury?
practice.e: A sharp creatinine rise soon after starting an ACE inhibitor in a vasculopath with a renal bruit suggests underlying renal artery stenosis.

steps.x: Underlying cause of an AKI.
Creatinine almost doubled after an ACE inhibitor, with atherosclerosis elsewhere.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Renal artery stenosis** unmasked by the ACE inhibitor.

elim: AIN gives rash, fever, eosinophilia; ACE inhibitors are not a typical cause.
Diabetic nephropathy is a slow decline with proteinuria.
No haematuria or systemic illness.
He is well and normotensive.

steps.x: **E. Renal artery stenosis.** Rule: creatinine jumps after ACE inhibitor = think RAS.

practice.stem: A 73 year old woman is admitted with pneumonia and sepsis. Her creatinine three months ago was 80 µmol/L. Her urine output has been 0.4 mL/kg/hour for 8 hours. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 100/60 mmHg.
practice.q: Which stage of acute kidney injury does she have?
practice.e: 252 ÷ 80 = 3.15 times baseline, so Stage 3. Stage by whichever criterion gives the highest stage; her urine output alone is Stage 1.

steps.x: Severity: stage the AKI.

clues: creatinine three months ago was 80 µmol/L
steps.x: Creatinine 252 vs 80 = **3.15 ×**; urine output gives only Stage 1.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Highest stage wins: **Stage 3**.

elim: She clearly meets AKI criteria.
Stage 1 fits her urine output, but you use the highest stage.
Stage 2 is 2 to 2.99 times baseline.
There is no Stage 4 AKI; that is CKD staging.

steps.x: **D. Stage 3.** Rule: 3 times baseline or more = Stage 3; use the worst criterion.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has a creatinine of 286 µmol/L, rising from 95 µmol/L two months ago. He has no recent illness, is not on new medication, and is clinically euvolaemic. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 146/86 mmHg. Bladder scan shows 80 mL.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging?
practice.e: Unexplained AKI needs a renal tract ultrasound within 24 hours to exclude obstruction (e.g. hydronephrosis).

steps.x: Initial imaging in AKI.
No pre-renal or drug cause: **unexplained** AKI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **USS KUB within 24 hours**.

elim: CT KUB is for suspected stones with colic.
Renograms assess split function later.
MRA looks at renal arteries; not first line, and gadolinium is a risk.
Plain X-ray misses obstruction.

steps.x: **E. Renal tract ultrasound.** Rule: unexplained AKI = USS KUB within 24 h.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man has 3 weeks of nasal crusting, nosebleeds and haemoptysis. His creatinine has risen from 88 µmol/L to 340 µmol/L over 10 days. Urine dipstick shows blood 3+ and protein 2+. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 158/94 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
practice.e: Haematuria and proteinuria with ENT and lung involvement suggest an intrinsic glomerular cause (ANCA vasculitis); the renal screen starts with ANCA.

steps.x: Find the cause of an intrinsic-looking AKI.
Rapid AKI with **active urine** and upper/lower airway disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Renal screen: **ANCA** (granulomatosis with polyangiitis).

elim: Cultures look for sepsis; this is a systemic inflammatory picture.
CT KUB is for stones.
Ultrasound excludes obstruction but will not identify vasculitis.
CK is for rhabdomyolysis.

steps.x: **A. ANCA.** Rule: blood and protein on dip in AKI = renal screen.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has 3 days of vomiting. His mouth is dry and his capillary refill time is 4 seconds. His pulse rate is 114 bpm and BP 88/52 mmHg. He takes ramipril, metformin and aspirin.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: He is hypovolaemic with pre-renal AKI: give IV 0.9% saline (and stop ramipril and metformin). Dialysis is not indicated.

steps.x: Initial management of AKI.
Hypovolaemic, hypotensive: **pre-renal**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV 0.9% saline** bolus, and stop DAMN drugs.

elim: 5% glucose does not stay in the circulation to restore volume.
Furosemide worsens hypovolaemia.
He is vomiting and shocked; oral fluids are not enough.
No AEIOU indication: K+ 5.4, no overload.

steps.x: **A. IV 0.9% sodium chloride.** Rule: dry pre-renal AKI = IV crystalloid.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman has acute kidney injury after a urinary tract infection. Her pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Her medications are aspirin 75 mg, atorvastatin, levothyroxine, ramipril and warfarin for atrial fibrillation.
practice.e: ACE inhibitors are a DAMN drug and should be withheld in AKI. Cardioprotective aspirin continues; warfarin is considered safe to continue with INR monitoring.

steps.x: Which drug to stop in AKI.
Use **DAMN**: diuretics, ACE inhibitor/ARB, metformin, NSAIDs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ramipril**.

elim: Low-dose cardioprotective aspirin is the NSAID exception.
Statins are not nephrotoxic here.
Levothyroxine is not renally harmful.
Warfarin is considered safe to continue; monitor INR.

steps.x: **D. Ramipril.** Rule: DAMN drugs stop; aspirin 75 mg and warfarin stay.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man has acute kidney injury from acute tubular necrosis. He has passed 50 mL of urine in 12 hours despite fluids and intravenous furosemide. He has bibasal crackles. His pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 150/90 mmHg and oxygen saturation 89% on 4 L/min oxygen. ECG (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Refractory hyperkalaemia >7, acidosis with pH <7.20 and refractory pulmonary oedema are AEIOU indications for dialysis (haemofiltration).

steps.x: Definitive management in refractory AKI.
K+ 7.4 with tented T waves, pH 7.14, refractory overload: three **AEIOU** triggers.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Renal replacement therapy** (dialysis / haemofiltration).

elim: Furosemide has already failed.
Bicarbonate adds sodium and fluid to an overloaded patient and is not definitive.
Calcium resonium is far too slow.
Salbutamol shifts potassium briefly; it is not definitive.

steps.x: **D. Renal replacement therapy.** Rule: refractory AEIOU = dialysis.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man has 4 days of vomiting and is clinically dehydrated. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. His urine is concentrated with a urine sodium of 8 mmol/L and osmolality of 640 mOsm/kg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for his low urinary sodium?
o: Sloughing of tubular cells into the urine
practice.e: Reduced renal perfusion activates RAAS, so aldosterone drives avid sodium and water retention: concentrated urine with low sodium.

steps.x: Mechanism of low urinary sodium.
Pre-renal: kidneys hypoperfused but tubules working.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **RAAS activation**: aldosterone retains sodium.

elim: Tubular damage (ATN) gives **high** urine sodium.
Obstruction is post-renal and not suggested.
ADH is **raised** in dehydration, concentrating urine.
Sloughed cells form casts in ATN.

steps.x: **A. RAAS activation.** Rule: pre-renal = working tubules holding on to sodium and water.
